newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen forces free kidnapped Russian journalists.
newsitem.headline: Chechen forces free kidnapped Russian journalists.

text.p: Authorities in Russia's breakaway region of Chechnya said on Tuesday that they had secured the release of two Russian journalists kidnapped in March by bandits.

Chechen Interior Minister Kazbek Makhashev said Olga Bagautdinova and Alexander Utrobin had been freed by the secessionist region's security forces. Makhashev said the two reporters were well but gave no further details.
Interfax news agency said an elite Chechen armed unit stormed an apartment where Bagautdinova was held and arrested two kidnappers after Utrobin escaped and contacted police.
One kidnapper managed to escape, the agency said. Chechen leaders have promised to execute kidnappers and to impose big jail terms on anyone who abets them.

The release marked a success for Chechen officials who are anxious to show Moscow the region is under control. A recent spate of violence has threatened negotiations to secure a lasting peace following the 1994-96 war between Chechnya and Russia.
Chechen President Aslan Maskhadov was quoted as saying he would "smear the walls" with a maverick guerrilla leader who claimed responsibility for two fatal bomb attacks in southern Russia last month.
Itar-Tass news agency quoted Makhashev as saying he hoped four other missing Russian journalists would soon be released. An Italian photographer was freed by kidnappers last month.

Kidnappings, usually for ransom, have become a common occurrence in Chechnya, where nearly all men are armed. The region was devastated during the 21-month war between Russian troops and pro-independence guerrillas that ended last August.
Russian and Chechen officials are now conducting difficult talks aimed at mapping out a new relationship between Moscow and the mainly Moslem North Caucasus territory.

Chechen First Deputy Prime Minister Movladi Udugov told Interfax on Tuesday after speaking to Russian Security Council secretary Ivan Rybkin that Russian President Boris Yeltsin would definitely meet Maskhadov in the first half of May.

"The war has not been ended, it has been put on hold. In order to put the final full stop to it the two presidents, Russian and Chechen, have to meet and sign a peace treaty," Maskhadov told Moskovskiye Novosti weekly.

Tass said Makhashev would speak by telephone later on Tuesday with Russian Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov on plans to set up a joint Russian-Chechen commission to investigate the recent spate of bombings in southern Russia.
Four people died and many more were injured in two bomb explosions in the towns of Armavir and Pyatigorsk last month.
Radical Chechen guerrilla commander Salman Raduyev has claimed responsibility for the attacks, which he said were a result of Moscow's refusal to recognise Chechen independence.
On Monday, Chechen officials said they had issued a warrant for Raduyev's arrest.
"I will smear Raduyev on the walls the day after we sign a peace treaty (with Moscow)," Maskhadov told Moskovskiye Novosti.

Kulikov told reporters that Raduyev would be arrested "at the first opportunity". Interior Ministry troops backed up by aircraft and tanks allowed Raduyev to slip through their lines when they had him surrounded in January 1996.
